listenings.text: I edit reports for a living, and the habit I spend most of my time fighting is the long sentence. Not because long sentences are wrong. A good long sentence is efficient. The documents attached to this email, the client mentioned in the minutes, the people working on the project: each of those phrases is a shorter version of a whole clause, and English readers process them very quickly. The problem starts when the writer loses track of who is doing what. My favorite example came from a report I edited last year. It said: having reviewed the figures, the budget looked unrealistic. Read it again. The budget did not review anything. Somebody did, and that somebody has disappeared from the sentence. So my advice is simple. Use the short forms as much as you like, but before you send anything, check that the first noun after the comma is the person who did the action.

I have written legal opinions for international clients for twenty-five years, and I have changed my mind about one thing. We still write pursuant to, and subject to, and hereinafter, and some of that language is genuinely useful, because it is precise. What I stopped doing is starting with it. A client reading in a second language should not have to decode three subordinate clauses to find out whether the answer is yes or no. So every opinion we send now opens with two sentences in plain English: the question, and our answer. The long sentence comes after that, for the lawyers on the other side and for the judge, if it ever gets that far. Clients have told me it is the first time they have read one of our opinions to the end. It costs us nothing, and it has probably prevented more disputes than any clause I have ever drafted.

reading.rtitle: Legal Opinion -- Late Delivery under the Supply Agreement
paras: You have asked us whether Valença Alimentos may terminate the Supply Agreement signed with Nordhaven B.V. on 3 March 2025 (hereinafter the Agreement), following the late delivery of the equipment ordered in June. In short, our view is that it may, subject to one condition explained below. This opinion is based only on the documents provided to us and does not cover any matter governed by Dutch law.

Clause 9.2 provides that any delivery made more than thirty days after the agreed date shall be deemed a material breach. The equipment, scheduled for delivery on 15 August, arrived on 29 September, forty-five days late. Having reviewed the delivery notes and the correspondence exchanged between the parties, we see no evidence that the delay was caused by an event of force majeure, as Nordhaven now claims.

Termination, however, is not automatic. Pursuant to Clause 14.1, the party wishing to terminate must first send a written notice setting forth the breach and allowing the other party fifteen days to remedy it. A notice sent by email alone will not be sufficient, since the Agreement requires delivery by courier to the address stated in the recitals. Any notice not complying with this requirement is likely to be construed as invalid.

Our recommendation is therefore to send a formal notice by courier this week, giving Nordhaven until 31 October to replace the equipment. If the breach is not remedied within that period, Valença will be entitled to terminate the Agreement and to claim the costs incurred as a result of the delay, with the proviso that any claim remains subject to the liability cap set forth in Clause 18. We would be happy to prepare the notice.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson as a realistic legal opinion (the companies and the agreement are fictional)

reading.prompt: What is the main conclusion of the opinion?
choices: Valença can terminate the Agreement today by sending Nordhaven a short email that explains the delay and the costs.
Valença may terminate, but only after a proper written notice that gives Nordhaven time to fix the breach.
The delay was caused by force majeure, so Valença cannot do anything.

items: The opinion also covers questions of Dutch law.
Paragraph 1: it does not cover any matter governed by Dutch law.
The equipment arrived more than thirty days after the agreed date.
Paragraph 2: scheduled for 15 August, it arrived on 29 September, forty-five days late.
An email is enough to start the termination process.
Paragraph 3: a notice sent by email alone will not be sufficient; it must go by courier.
Any claim for costs is limited by the liability cap.
Paragraph 4: any claim remains subject to the liability cap set forth in Clause 18.
